prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Animula, vagula, blandula. Life! I know not what thou art, But know that thou and I must part; And when, or how, or where we met, I own to me’s a secret yet. But this I know, when thou art fled, Where’er they lay these limbs, this head, No clod so valueless shall be, As all that then remains of me. O whither, whither dost thou fly, Where bend unseen thy trackless course, And in this strange divorce, Ah tell where I must seek this compound I? To the vast ocean of empyreal flame, From whence thy essence came, Dost thou thy flight pursue, when freed From matter’s base encumbering weed? Or dost thou, hid from sight, Wait, like some spell-bound knight, Through blank oblivious years th’ appointed hour, To break thy trance and reassume thy power? Yet canst thou without thought or feeling be? O say what art thou, when no more thou ’rt thee? Life! we’ve been long together, Through pleasant and through cloudy weather; ’Tis hard to part when friends are dear; Perhaps ’t will cost a sigh, a tear; Then steal away, give little warning, Choose thine own time; Say not Good night, but in some brighter clime Bid me Good morning.

outputs.L1:
*Animula, vagula, blandula.*

Life! I know not what thou art,  
But know that thou and I must part;  
And when, or how, or where we met,  
I own, to me, is a secret yet.

But this I know: when thou art fled,  
Where’er they lay these limbs, this head,  
No clod so valueless shall be  
As all that then remains of me.

O whither, whither dost thou fly?  
Where bends, unseen, thy trackless course?  
And in this strange divorce,  
Ah, tell me where I must seek this compound “I.”

To the vast ocean of empyreal flame,  
From whence thy essence came,  
Dost thou thy flight pursue when freed  
From matter’s base, encumbering weed?

Or dost thou, hidden from sight,  
Wait, like some spellbound knight,  
Through blank, oblivious years, th’ appointed hour  
To break thy trance and reassume thy power?

Yet canst thou be without thought or feeling?  
O say, what art thou when no more thou art thee?

Life! We’ve been long together,  
Through pleasant and through cloudy weather;  
’Tis hard to part when friends are dear—  
Perhaps ’twill cost a sigh, a tear.

Then steal away; give little warning;  
Choose thine own time.  
Say not “Good night,” but, in some brighter clime,  
Bid me “Good morning.”
outputs.L2:
Little soul—wandering, gentle, dear.

Life, I cannot say what you are; I know only that someday we must separate. When, where, and by what means we first came together remains a mystery to me. Yet I am certain of this: once you have departed, wherever my head and limbs are placed, even the most worthless lump of earth will have greater value than whatever is left of me.

Where will you go? Along what invisible, unmarked path will you travel? When this strange division occurs, where should the united self that is “I” be sought? Once released from the lowly, burdensome covering of matter, will you return to the immense sea of heavenly fire from which your essence first arose? Or will you remain unseen, like an enchanted knight, passing through empty years of forgetfulness until the destined moment arrives for you to awaken and recover your strength?

But can you exist without sensation or thought? Tell me: when you are no longer yourself, what will you be?

Life, you and I have shared many years, through bright days and troubled ones alike. Dear friends do not separate easily; our farewell may bring a sigh or even a tear. So leave quietly and with little notice, choosing the moment for yourself. Do not tell me “Good night.” Instead, in some more radiant world, greet me with “Good morning.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker acknowledges that life is a profound mystery, yet accepts one certainty: death will eventually separate life from the physical body. Once that vital force has departed, the body will lose its meaning and become nothing more than worthless remains.

The poem then reflects on the uncertain fate of the soul. The speaker wonders whether it returns to a divine source, falls into a dormant state, or continues to exist in some form beyond human understanding. Although no definite answer is offered, these questions reveal a deep hope that death is not simply an ending.

Life itself is portrayed as a cherished and faithful companion. It has remained with the speaker through moments of happiness as well as periods of hardship, creating a bond that makes the thought of separation especially painful. For this reason, the speaker asks that death come gently, without unnecessary suffering. Ultimately, the poem expresses the hope that this temporary separation will lead to reunion in a brighter and more peaceful afterlife.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the enduring mystery of what happens to the human soul after death. Confronted with mortality, the speaker considers several possibilities but cannot determine which, if any, is true. Perhaps consciousness returns to the divine source from which it came, becoming part of a greater spiritual existence. Perhaps the soul remains in a state of rest, waiting for resurrection and the restoration of life. Or perhaps death brings complete extinction, and the individual self simply disappears. These questions reveal both the speaker’s spiritual longing and an honest awareness that the fate of the soul lies beyond human knowledge.

Yet the poem does not end in despair. Instead of presenting death only as a frightening conclusion, it imagines it as a gentle but painful separation between those who must depart and those who remain. The mood becomes one of tenderness, grief, and cautious consolation. Although certainty is impossible, hope still offers emotional and spiritual comfort: what appears to be a final farewell may prove temporary. Death may open the way to a brighter existence in which loved ones are reunited and loss is overcome. Thus, the poem accepts uncertainty while preserving faith in the possibility that separation will ultimately become reunion.
outputs.L5:
**Animula**

Animula—little soul—moves quietly through life, gathering moments as a bird gathers threads for its nest. It knows the warmth of morning light, the weight of grief, the sudden joy of a familiar voice.

Life asks it to grow, to lose, to begin again. But the soul is never entirely prepared. It trembles before change and clings to what must pass. Still, it continues—small, wandering, tender—carrying within itself the courage to love a world that cannot last.
